headline: Andrew Coleman says Harvey Norman is good value, describing it as a property company and operator rather than a pure retailer
reasoning: Coleman argues that Harvey Norman's identity as a property company and business model operator rather than a traditional retailer has been well understood by the market for over a decade. He notes Harvey Norman's historic 10-year earnings growth rate of 4.2% per annum is just ahead of inflation, consistent with its property-retailer model, and the latest result of 4.9% growth is well within business-as-usual range. He considers the stock good value at current levels.
quote: Harvey Norman is more a property company and an operator of a business model than they are actually a retailer. And that's probably been pretty well understood, I think, by most in the market for at least the last decade and a half while Jerry and his wife have made that very clear. I think what was interesting, we were talking before about, was this season just business as usual? Well, Harvey Norman's historic 10-year growth rate of earnings has been 4.2% per annum, just faster than inflation, in line with that property retailer model. And what did they report this year? 4.9%? So well within business as usual changes. I would say the stock's really good value at the moment.

headline: Andrew Coleman would sell AMP citing high debt, limited moats and a quarter-century of capital destruction
reasoning: AMP has been a capital destroyer for Australian investors for 25 years despite originally being one of the 20 largest companies in Australia with a great brand name. Debt to equity remains too high, growth is choppy and dependent on new strategies, and it faces increasing competition in financial advice, platforms, fund management and superannuation. Coleman believes there are better companies both within and outside financial services and places AMP straight in the sell basket.
quote: I think AMP has the classic problem of a business that has limited moats and a strategy that seems to be to try and follow the river to where it looks good next as a result it's been a capital killer for Australian investors for I don't know the last 25 years despite originally starting off as one of you know the 20 largest companies in this country with one of the great brand names today in debt to equity still way too high growth is choppy and comes from new strategies they've got more and more competitors whether that's in financial advice platforms fund management superannuation to me there's got to be better places to put your money I would think if you in any sector let alone financial services you know if you want the financial services sector there are better companies that AMP and if you don't want financial services then I'll bear a better companies than financial services so from that point of view I think for our members it's straight into the cell basket.

headline: Sees as a consistent compounder but outside circle of competence
reasoning: Harvey Norman has delivered a 10-year historic earnings growth rate of 4.2% per annum, slightly above inflation, and this year reported 4.9% in line with that trajectory. It is essentially a property company as much as a retailer, giving investors dual cyclical exposure. At a PE of 10-11 it is not expensive, but the inherent cyclicality of both retail and property means it does not meet Team Invest's requirement for near-certain earnings growth year after year. It is a wonderful business but does not make the top 20-30 holdings Coleman wants to own.
quote: I think Harvey Norman is more a property company and an operator of a business model than they are actually a retailer and that's probably been pretty well understood I think by most in the market for at least the last decade and a half. I think what was interesting we were talking before about was this season just business as usual. Well Harvey Norman's historic 10-year growth rate of earnings has been 4.2% per annum just faster than inflation sort of in line with that property retailer model and what did they report this year 4.9 so well within business as usual changes. I think from an investor who wants to own Harvey Norman point of view you've got to ask the two classic questions which is number one is this inside your circle of competence because retail and property are both inherently cyclical so you're getting both exposures there so if you're someone like us at Team Invest who wants to be virtually certain earnings are going to rise year after year with great stability Harvey Norman doesn't quite meet our requirements but having said that it's not far off and it continues to print money at a slightly faster rate than inflation so you can buy it like you can at the moment on a PE of around 10-11 it may not be about investment but bear in mind always it's got to be in the top 20 or 30 you want to own and for me and probably for our members Harvey Norman doesn't meet that requirement but still a wonderful business.

headline: Team Invest exited Mineral Resources after it transitioned from crushing company to miner, citing increased cyclicality and key-man risk
reasoning: Team Invest was formerly a top-10 shareholder in Mineral Resources when it operated primarily as a crushing services company, which fitted their stability and moat-based investment criteria. As the company shifted toward mining its cyclicality and key-man risk around Chris Ellison grew, and the team eventually placed it in the too-hard basket. Coleman acknowledges the exit was well-timed but maintains the underlying risks have not changed.
quote: our membership used to be in the top 10 shareholders of Min res for many years back when it was a crushing company and and was therefore more understandable at less cyclical now of course it's more into mining and so there's a cyclicality and a risk element that you you touched on on the intro I think that challenge if you are an investor in Min resources is twofold the first is that clearly the reason that Min resources has been such an incredibly well-run company for the last 25 years relies upon the person that Ben kept mentioning of course being Chris Ellison the sort of founding guiding entrepreneurial leader and the challenge is like many fun founding guiding entrepreneurial leaders he doesn't necessarily decisions that you would see coming... we've had a tendency over time that when you have to talk about a company to understand it that much the odds are that information asymmetry will end against you now we were lucky it as it turns out we timed our exit well the company has since performed very well beyond its problems but those problems are still there.

headline: Andrew Coleman sells Mineral Resources citing key-man risk around Chris Ellison and inherent cyclicality
reasoning: Team Invest was once a top-10 shareholder in Mineral Resources when it was primarily a crushing company, but moved it to the too-hard basket as it became more of a mining company with greater cyclicality. The fundamental concern is key-man risk around founder-CEO Chris Ellison whose decisions are not always predictable or aligned with shareholders. The company requires too much ongoing analysis to understand what is happening at any given time, signalling high information asymmetry. Coleman acknowledges the recent strong performance but believes the same underlying risks remain.
quote: clearly the reason that Min resources has been such an incredibly well-run company for the last 25 years relies upon the person that Ben kept mentioning of course being Chris Ellison the sort of founding guiding entrepreneurial leader and the challenge is like many fun founding guiding entrepreneurial leaders he doesn't necessarily decisions that you would see coming which on the one hand if he is wonderful but on the other hand it can sometimes result in a mismatch between the decisions he takes for his and the company's benefit and the decisions that shareholders may wish to be taken and so as a result you you will often find yourself as a shareholder in that classic state of uncertainty around where is this company going who is benefiting and will that be me and as a result we just started to move it into our too hard basket and stopped covering it really because it became all we could talk about in our meetings was what was going on in Min res right because there's so much always going on so we've had a tendency over time that when you have to talk about a company to understand it that much the odds are that information asymmetry will end against you.

headline: Andrew Coleman notes Sims benefits from AI-driven IT recycling tailwind but earnings uncertainty keeps it outside his circle
reasoning: Coleman sees Sims as a well-run business benefiting from a second-order tailwind from the IT and AI boom, where the infrastructure support services often benefit more than first-order technology players without needing the same capex. However, he cannot predict where Sims' earnings will be next year or the year after given the cyclicality, so it does not fit Team Invest's requirement for near-certain compounding. He advises existing holders to assess whether it is within their circle of competence before deciding to hold or take profits.
quote: I think Ben nailed it I mean it's a cyclical industry it has significant what we would call in finance operational leverage you know every extra bit of volume it puts through every extra dollar it gets for that volume flows straight to the bottom line and conversely every volume that's missing goes straight out of the bottom line right so as a result it will always have pretty choppy results but I think it's been a very well-run business you know and it's clearly benefiting right now from that sort of second order tailwind of what we're seeing in IT and I think maybe that's the thing that's really interesting for me as a viewer of it whilst I wouldn't be particularly interested in owning Sims or our members would be particularly interested because we can't be virtually certain about its earnings growth it's just yet again that truism that the ones who make the most in any rush any boom tends not to be the first-order players you know the ones inventing the technology it's often the second and third order suppliers.

headline: Avoids the property development sector as too hard for compounding investors
reasoning: Property development by its nature requires constant recycling of capital: operators take risk to improve assets, then must sell or monetise and start again rather than compounding returns. This means investors face an ever-compounding element of risk rather than reward. The bigger the company gets the larger the bets required and the higher execution risk becomes. Stockland's 10-year results demonstrate this with every good year followed by excess risk in the next. Coleman also notes most Australians already have heavy property exposure through their own homes and investment properties, making additional listed property exposure redundant.
quote: the challenge in property development and property ownership from a compounding point of view if you want to think of investing as the goal of compounding growth year after year until hopefully an infinite time horizon though none of us will ever live that long is that in the property development game what they call a pipeline we as an investor have to call starting over because the nature of the business is to take something unloved put risk and capital into it to make it better and then having completed that exercise rather than sitting back and enjoying the fruits of your labor you have to either sell it or monetize it and then go again and so as an investor you are going to experience in the property sector in general in Stockland is no no unique beast in that a constantly compounding element of risk rather than reward because the bigger they get the bigger the gambles they have to take the higher the execution risk comes the more likelihood that you can't get one part of that pipeline right.

headline: Andrew Coleman avoids Zip and the buy now pay later sector as structurally dangerous lending to those banks won't touch
reasoning: Buy now pay later, private credit, subprime and B-grade lending all share the same fundamental flaw: they lend to people or companies that banks will not lend to, at rates those borrowers would never pay at a bank. As long as the economy is strong repayments continue, but at the first sign of weakness the customers in that socioeconomic band default disproportionately. External investors cannot properly evaluate the loan book quality and therefore face catastrophic information asymmetry: making one to two percent on each loan when it goes well and losing 100% when it goes badly.
quote: the challenge with any business model whether it's a buy now pay later whether it's a B grade lender whether it's private credit that involves you taking risk by giving people money who can't get that money from other easier avenues is that as long as the economy continues strongly you're probably okay that money will be repaid people don't tend to take on debts they have no intention of ever repaying the challenge is that as soon as there's any weakness in the economy the customers who repay the least the quickest are those of course who are in that socio-economic band if it's individuals or companies in that lower level of earnings band who couldn't borrow money from banks... by now pay later private credit B grade finance subprime lending whatever you want to call it it changes its name every few years is all about lending to people the banks won't lend to at rates that they would never have to pay at the bank and that means it's always a house of cards because the more you grow the more risk you take on that somewhere in your lending book is a big cohort of customers that if something goes wrong they won't be repaying.

headline: Andrew Coleman warns Australian private credit sector faces systemic risk akin to 2008
reasoning: Coleman believes private credit funds offering elevated yields relative to fixed income must by definition be lending to borrowers who cannot access cheaper capital. He sees widespread problems across the sector in Australia and globally and draws an explicit parallel with the conditions that led to the 2008 financial crisis. He believes private credit as a whole has a long way to fall.
quote: we have cockroaches galore in our private capital sector in Australia let alone globally this is yet another example of 2008 I think just playing out again I don't think Centuria will be the biggest loser there by the way so I think if you're in Centuria you're probably in the more safer categories but I think private credit as a whole has a long way to fall from here.

headline: Andrew Coleman would sell Centuria Capital warning of systemic private credit risk and cockroaches in the sector
reasoning: Coleman warns that the beauty of private capital is that no one knows what it is worth until someone refuses to buy it. Any fund offering investors substantially higher yield than fixed income must be lending to higher-risk borrowers. He sees widespread problems in private credit in Australia and globally, likening it to a replay of 2008, and believes private credit as a whole has a long way to fall. He rates Centuria as one of the better operators in the space but would not own it given the sector-wide risk.
quote: the beauty of private capital is that no one knows what it's worth until someone else refuses to buy it and I think Centuria is no different to everyone else in that space you know if you are going to offer your investors substantially higher yield than they can get on fixed income elsewhere that means you have to be lending to people who prepared to pay you a higher yield than perhaps their risk implies to someone who doesn't know the underlying portfolio I think Centuria is one of the better operators in this space but we have cockroaches galore in our private capital sector in Australia let alone globally this is yet another example of 2008 I think just playing out again I don't think Centuria will be the biggest loser there by the way so I think if you're in Centuria you're probably in the more safer categories but I think private credit as a whole has a long way to fall from here.

headline: Andrew Coleman rates Data 3 a buy as managed service provider perfectly positioned to benefit from enterprise AI adoption
reasoning: Data 3 has delivered return on equity above 40% for the last 10 years and now well above 50%, with earnings per share growing double digits for a decade with high stability and low debt. As enterprises buy more AI and software licenses they need a managed service provider to sit in the middle, and Data 3 clips that ticket, creating a significant structural tailwind. The stock is on a PE of 31, which is not as cheap as it was in the teens where Team Invest added to their position, but Coleman still considers it a buy because the business quality is exceptional. He views valuation as the only question for an otherwise near-certain compounder.
quote: the last 10 years return on equity above 40% these days well above 50% earnings per share growing double digits for the last 10 years with an incredibly high degree of stability low-debt wonderful management team and we've been talking about AI and data centers they are the managed service provider to the users of those AIs and data centers so we're data three of course it's in the ecosystem is large governments and large corporate users who need someone to manage their IT on an ever increasing basis as they buy more and more of these AI licenses and software licenses well data three is the one who sits in the middle and clips that ticket so as a result huge tailwinds behind them I'm gonna sound like a broken record in the sense of having talked about data three lots on this program but I think all I'll say is this result was another truism that wonderful companies with wonderful moats keep being virtually certain to grow their earnings at the same stable double-digit rates they did before and as an investor that is music to your ears on a PE of 31 it's probably not as cheap as it was recently it had got our way down into the teens and we bought some more there but it still probably looks like a buy to me.

headline: Andrew Coleman sells Star Entertainment as two insolvent entities combined are no solution for shareholders
reasoning: The horse shareholders are backing to turn Star around is Bally's Entertainment Group as the large shareholder, but Bally's is now facing its own solvency scandal in the United States. Combining two insolvent entities creates a mathematically negative outcome for shareholders. Coleman has no interest in the stock.
quote: I think that the biggest challenge for me with Star other than the realities of what's happening at Star is that the horse you are backing as a Star shareholder to turn it around right now of course is Bally's Entertainment Group as the the larger shareholder and Bally's themselves are in a big scandal overnight now in the United States around their own solvency so putting two insolvent together like with mathematics if you multiply two negative numbers but for shareholder not to be very positive.

headline: Andrew Coleman avoids 2S as too hard with regulatory uncertainty making valuation impossible despite quality management
reasoning: Coleman places 2S squarely in the too-hard basket due to the regulatory uncertainty making it impossible to make any call on what is likely to happen. He acknowledges founder David Tio is a serial successful entrepreneur and that the business will likely succeed eventually, but investing requires having confidence in the price paid for a share in that future, which is impossible here. At a PE of 52 times, or about 25 times after cash, it is not the right price to pay for a business with this level of uncertainty.
quote: I think it's just another one of those companies that if you put it in Buffett's terms of you know there's a yes basket and no basket and a too hard basket this is in the too hard basket as Ben points out there's just too much uncertainty I think for an investor to make any call on what's likely to happen I would say in the positive side of the column though you know David Tio to that to us and before that with all of his various other entities he is really at one of those serial successful entrepreneurs in this part of the market so the odds are they will make a success of whatever the business is but unfortunately as an investor you're not backing just the success of the business that is one of the key ingredients but you're also backing the price or having to make a call on the price you pay for that share of that business and that's I think the element where you have difficulty with to us do I think one day to us will be a successful business probably with its management team it'll eventually get through these regulatory hurdles buddies a PE of 52 times call it 25 times after cash the right price to pay for a business with that level of uncertainty.

headline: Andrew Coleman holds Integral Diagnostics as high-quality business but PE of 35x looks full
reasoning: Integral Diagnostics has a relatively dominant position in radiology, which suffered COVID-related headwinds in user numbers but is structurally stable and growing. The business has strong moats and near-certain future cash flows. However, the stock has returned from a very low PE to around 35 times earnings, which Coleman considers a bit full for a value investor. He would like to own it as a long-term investor but the current price prevents a buy call.
quote: It has a relatively dominant position in radiology radiology of course has suffered some headwinds recently of the sort of long hangover from covered in terms of user numbers and you've seen that in their competitors as well but at the end of the day we need radiology services it's a stable business that grows at a pretty stable rate the only question is around the price that you have to pay for that and like all medical stocks it was on a very high PE and then got to a very low PE and it's returned to a PE of about 35 times so the only reason I'm not going to put a buy on IDX is the fact that that price as a PE multiple is probably a bit full for a value investor like us at Team Invest but it's the kind of business that you want to own as a long-term investor because it's got you know strong boats and virtual certainty of its future cash flows so I hold for now.

headline: TeamInvest's Andrew Coleman sees Worley as good value near technical lows, recommending dollar-cost averaging over a long time horizon
reasoning: Coleman describes Worley as a large, stable global engineering consultancy doing $11 billion in sales and $400 million in profits, having grown earnings at 13% per annum over 10 years. He notes the PCM (project and construction management) business has cyclical earnings sensitivity to commodity cycles. He says the company is well-positioned for energy transition and data centre projects. While it doesn't meet TeamInvest's stability requirements, he views it as good value at current levels near the bottom of its technical range, recommending a patient, dollar-cost averaging approach.
quote: I think Warley is a very wonderful Australian success story. It's one of the largest engineering consultancies in the world. Today it does about 11 billion in sales and 400 million in profits. So it's a very large, stable organisation in that sense. Over the last 10 years, it's been able to grow earnings at an average of 13 percent per annum with the kind of stability, though, that you would expect from commodity exposure... I think this is probably a really good value down here, as you can see from a technical standpoint, is, you know, towards the bottom of the range. But you probably want to take it on a long term timeline, though, and I'd say probably just dollar cost average. I don't think there's any rush.

headline: Team Invest's Andrew Coleman rates Super Retail Group a hold at 12.5x PE, sees better entry price ahead despite quality franchise
reasoning: Coleman notes Super Retail is now trading at a PE of 12.5x, which is approaching the range where a value investor in a quality, consistently growing retailer should become interested. He acknowledges the company grows earnings faster than inflation and dominates its niche. However, he believes a better price will be available and flags that the five-year strategic plan presentation was heavy on marketing buzzwords, which is uncharacteristic of the business. He would give it a buy without the macro headwinds but is cautious on putting new cash to work now.
quote: You can now buy them on a PE of 12.5. So to Mark's comment before about as a value investor, things are starting to look pretty rosy. 12.5 may not be the kind of super exciting for a retailer. You can often get them high single digits, very low double digits, but it's getting right back towards the trading range where a value investor looking at a business with this kind of track record should start to get quite excited. I'm going to say a hold for today, because I think you'll get it at a better price... 12.5 overall is not a bad PE to be paying for a company that grows earnings consistently faster than inflation and dominates its niche.
